title: 🎙️ Science, Wonder & the Natural World
description: Today we look at scientific discovery and the natural world — from ecology and wildlife research to astronomy and deep-sea biology. We're grounding these stories in the landscapes and living systems of the Cariboo: what salmon runs, boreal forest research, or species-at-risk studies tell us about the wild places we live beside. We're after stories that inspire curiosity and wonder about how the world works. - Daily themed article selection for podcast generation

_podcast.theme_description: Today we look at scientific discovery and the natural world — from ecology and wildlife research to astronomy and deep-sea biology. We're grounding these stories in the landscapes and living systems of the Cariboo: what salmon runs, boreal forest research, or species-at-risk studies tell us about the wild places we live beside. We're after stories that inspire curiosity and wonder about how the world works.
_podcast.theme_scoring_prompt: Rate how well this article fits the theme 'Science, Wonder & the Natural World' — scientific discovery, ecology, natural phenomena, and the curiosity-driven study of living systems. Strong fits include: wildlife biology and species research, ecology studies and biodiversity findings, watershed and salmon research relevant to BC, astronomy and space science, new species discoveries, citizen science projects, natural history stories, wildfire science and forest ecology, climate science findings (not just policy), geology, evolution, and deep-time Earth stories, and any scientific research grounded in BC or Cariboo landscapes and ecosystems. Prefer articles that convey genuine curiosity and discovery — the 'how' and 'why' of the natural world. Score 70–90 for: prehistoric life and palaeontology (ancient oceans, Cretaceous ecology, deep-time species), new species discoveries in ocean or remote environments, deep-sea biology, evolutionary biology findings, natural history stories with a strong sense of wonder, and field research grounded in BC ecosystems. Penalise (score 0–30): consumer health and pharmaceutical research without ecology or natural-world context; pure policy and advocacy news; technology business stories without a science or ecology angle; human interest and viral news without scientific substance; geopolitical and crime news. Score 0-100 where 100 is a perfect thematic match and 0 is completely unrelated.

items.title: [Fast Company] The Transportation Department is recruiting gamers to solve its air traffic controller shortage
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

For more than a decade there has been a shortage of air traffic controllers in the U.S., which has resulted in flight delays and increased risks for air travelers. And the Department of Transportation (DOT) is looking to video game enthusiasts to help fill those gaps.

The DOT first launched a program in 2025 to recruit gamers. Now Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy is extolling the success of that program on social media.

Reaching out to gamers, he wrote on X, has resulted in the DOT meeting 94% of its hiring goal for new controllers, a record-setting pace. More than 2,000 people have been hired, he said, with candidates “reaching the Academy quicker than any class before them.”

To be clear, that doesn’t mean those gamers are already guiding actual aircraft through takeoff and landing. Even with the streamlined hiring process the DOT has enacted, it takes two years for a trainee to complete the air traffic controller training program. And roughly one in three trainees drops out before completing the program.

Still, gamers remain an area of interest for the DOT as it looks to fill empty seats. In a past interview, Duffy said “they problem solve. They’re spatially aware. They do multiple things at the same time.”

For the gamers, there are definitely some advantages and disadvantages of taking this job. On the upside, the pay is good. The median salary in 2024 was $144,580—and all you need, education-wise, is an associate’s degree. However, those paychecks haven’t been steady of late, thanks to government shutdowns. Controllers were ordered to work without pay for 43 days last year (with back salary given when the government reopened). And hundreds of Federal Aviation Administration jobs have been cut in the past two years.

There’s also the job itself. Air traffic controllers have one of the most stressful occupations in the country. Decisions are literally life and death. The equipment they rely on is often outdated. Many work six days a week. And because of the staffing crisis, controllers are often handling several more planes than they expected to.

Roughly 20% of trainees fail to certify as a controller at the first assigned facility—and some facilities have a much higher washout rate. And while it’s easy to rage quit a game, the stakes are much different with a real-world plane.

Shifting numbers

While Duffy celebrated reaching 94% of the hiring goal, it’s worth noting that the FAA, in May, cut its staffing target for air traffic controllers from 14,633 to 12,563. It said, at the time, that modernized staffing models were behind the change. But the agency actually increased the amount of time employees spent managing air traffic, to avoid the overtime bills the FAA ran up in 2024, which totaled approximately $200 million.

The substantial number of hires is also raising eyebrows because, traditionally, less than 10% of applicants are accepted into the training program, according to the FAA. The higher acceptance figures could be because of the new fully automated qualification process the FAA adopted last year. That process allowed applicants to proceed individually, rather than in a group. It also made the required comprehensive medical and security checks concurrent, though that doesn’t necessarily account for the large acceptance level.

Even if it did, the FAA has its work cut out in the years ahead. Hiring goals for 2026, 2027 and 2028 are all staggered higher than the previous year. And the GAO reports that the attrition rate from applicants for an air traffic controller role to a fully successful hire (passing all clearance approvals, finishing the academy and becoming fully certified) is incredibly high. Just 2% of all applications fully complete the training process.

Over the past decade, the number of air traffic controllers in the U.S. has declined by 6%, while the number of flights has increased by 10%. Even with the FAA’s successful wooing of gamers to fill the jobs, there’s no definitive sign, at the moment, that either number’s trajectory will change.

items.title: [Kagi Small Web] Introducing the Micro.blog PDS
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

I’ve started rolling out an AT Protocol PDS — personal data server — for new Micro.blog users. In the Bluesky world, a PDS is what stores your posts, follows, photos, and other data from apps. In the same way that creating an account on Micro.blog automatically gives you a fediverse handle, I wanted people to be able to create a Micro.blog account and have everything they needed to sign into Bluesky.

If you’re already using Bluesky, there aren’t currently any advantages to using Micro.blog’s PDS. We run the PDS reference implementation, with various new UI bits in the Micro.blog frontend for managing your account. You won’t even see the PDS option if you already have Bluesky cross-posting configured for your blog.

I’ve updated the account page so that both fediverse and atmosphere settings feel at home together:

I’m inspired by all the developer activity in the atmosphere. Everything from blogging apps like Leaflet and Pckt, to photo sharing, even puzzles. All of these apps store data on the PDS and require no changes to work with Micro.blog.

Domain names have always been a fundamental part of Micro.blog. When new users opt to use Micro.blog’s PDS, their domain name becomes their Bluesky handle. They can then immediately sign into Bluesky with their own domain name without creating an account on Bluesky. It feels a little like using IndieAuth to sign in with your blog.

It’s early and I’m not entirely sure where all of this is going. But ever since Bluesky added support for an external PDS, it has felt like a missing piece in Micro.blog hosting. I’m happy to fill that in and see what happens.

items.title: [Fast Company] More than half of workers would take a pay cut for job security
items.content_html:
🔭 ✏️

Employees in 2026 are seriously worried about how unstable their jobs may be. So worried, in fact, that more than half say they’d willingly swap part of their paycheck for greater job security.

According to a new survey from Monster, which recently polled 1,020 U.S. employees across a range of industries, job security is of the utmost importance to workers today. While earning a decent living is massively important, as the cost of living soars, most workers would still trade a chunk of their salary for the promise of continued work. A whopping 54% of those surveyed said they’d take a pay cut for greater job stability. 

Exactly how large of a pay cut workers would trade varied. The survey found that more than a quarter (28%) would accept a salary reduction of at least 5%, including 11% who said they’d take a salary reduction of 10% to know their job was secure.

Additionally, workers would also trade other massively important benefits to know their job was safe, too. Twenty-six percent said they’d take reduced bonuses or incentives, as well as workplace perks or benefits. Even the almighty flexibility was on the table, with 23% saying they’d even give up the option to work remotely. Meanwhile, 17% said they’d willingly pay higher health insurance costs.

Not everyone values job security over every other workplace benefit, however. 

Thirty-nine percent say they wouldn’t give up their salary, remote work, their bonuses, or anything at all to ensure their job was safe. Still, the large majority (61%) feel that holding onto their job is the most important offering on the table, as that percentage of workers would give up at least one workplace incentive to stay employed.

The latest stats show just how important job security is to Americans today. And given recent job loss data, the numbers add up. 

A recent Labor Department report showed that U.S. employers unexpectedly cut 23,000 jobs last month. After Labor Department revisions, there were 103,000 jobs taken off payrolls in May and June. And while unemployment fell to 4.1%, it only happened because 264,000 Americans stopped looking for work altogether.

Still, job insecurity is hardly a new concern for Americans. Last year, the American Psychological Association’s 2025 Work in America survey found that more than half of American workers (54%) said concerns about their workplace stability had a “significant impact” on how stressed they were. 

“When people feel their jobs are at risk, it creates a sense of uncertainty that can affect every aspect of their lives,” Dr. Arthur C. Evans Jr., APA’s chief executive officer, said in a news release at the time.

Evans continued: “This cultural moment is threatening workers’ sense of stability, control and ability to meet their basic needs. And feelings of insecurity at work and poor mental health can amplify each other in a vicious cycle.”
